title: Direct simulation of LiNi₀.₈Mn₀.₁Co₀.₁O₂ transport properties using an efficient and accurate machine learning potential
abstract: The rate capability of layered lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) cathode materials is decisive for high-power applications such as fast charging, yet the mechanisms governing lithium-ion transport in NMC remain insufficiently understood, both experimentally and computationally. In this work, an efficient and accurate machine learning potential (MLP) was developed for LiNi₀.₈Mn₀.₁Co₀.₁O₂ (NMC811) to enable direct large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of lithium self-diffusion. The workflow uses a fine-tuned MACE (Message Passing Atomic Cluster Expansion) foundation model as a structure generator together with an active learning strategy applied to a near-ground-state dataset, which allows a reliable MLP to be constructed in a data-efficient manner from a limited number of density functional theory (DFT) reference calculations. MD simulations based on this potential preserve the accuracy of DFT while overcoming its time and length scale limitations, and were used to predict lithium diffusion coefficients in NMC811. This record contains the DFT reference data used for direct force training and testing of the artificial neural network (ANN) interatomic potential with the atomic energy network (ænet) and ænet-PyTorch packages (https://github.com/atomisticnet/aenet-PyTorch). Each data file contains an atomic structure together with its energy and atomic forces in XCrySDen Structure Format (XSF). The structure and content of the archive are described in README.md.

title: Machine learning-driven inverse design of high-hardness multi-principal element alloys through symbolic regression
abstract: Conventional trial-and-error metallurgical approaches fail to efficiently develop high-hardness multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), limited by poor physical interpretability of existing machine learning (ML) hardness prediction models and the lack of targeted inverse composition optimization. This work establishes a closed-loop physics-informed ML framework integrating symbolic regression (SR), CatBoost surrogate modelling and multi-metaheuristic optimization to address the two core bottlenecks. A comprehensive descriptor library is constructed by integrating elemental fractions, pymatgen-derived atomic physicochemical properties and classical Hume-Rothery metallurgical parameters, which quantitatively captures lattice distortion, electronic effects and phase transformation mechanisms governing alloy hardness. Genetic programming-based symbolic regression automatically extracts three nonlinear descriptors that encode standardized physicochemical variables, reducing the original 39-dimensional feature space by 33% and remarkably elevating predictive accuracy. The SR-enhanced CatBoost model achieves a test-set coefficient of determination R 2 = 0.885 and RMSE = 77.2 HV, far outperforming traditional semi-empirical formulas and baseline ML models. SHAP analysis verifies that the three SR features contribute 52% of total predictive weight, explicitly elucidating non-monotonic hardening responses including hardness saturation under excessive atomic size mismatch and the trade-off between bulk modulus and dislocation storage capacity. A triangulated inverse design pipeline combining genetic algorithm, particle swarm optimization and whale optimization algorithm is deployed to maximize Vickers hardness under four- and five-principal-element constraints. Cross-algorithm convergence shows stability of the search under a shared surrogate rather than global optimality. The 22 candidates that clear the physical screen and the domain test span 716.6-783.1 HV. Refractory W and Mo act as primary strengthening elements, while moderate Al addition enables simultaneous lightweighting and possible precipitation hardening. This integrated framework unifies interpretable forward hardness prediction, mechanistic analysis and targeted compositional inverse design, drastically cutting experimental screening costs. Future research will incorporate processing and microstructural variables to realize multi-objective optimization balancing hardness, density and ductility.

title: Universal machine learning force fields for materials simulation: From model construction to complex-system applications
abstract: Abstract Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) can achieve first-principles accuracy within validated chemical and configurational domains while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to classical force fields for atomistic materials simulations. Currently, MLFFs are evolving from system-specific models toward universal MLFFs. This review summarizes recent progress in universal MLFFs from data construction, model architecture, fine-tuning strategy, physical priors, and complex-system applications. We focus on three reliability bottlenecks: potential energy surface softening due to biased near-equilibrium pretraining data, catastrophic forgetting during downstream fine-tuning, and insufficient treatment of long-range electrostatics, dispersion, and polarization. Representative datasets and benchmarks are discussed together with typical universal MLFFs. We further review forgetting-aware fine-tuning strategies, physics-enhanced frameworks and polarizable long-range models, as well as representative applications in battery electrolytes, solid-state interfaces, ferroelectric phase transitions, phonons, defects and thermal transport. Finally, future directions are discussed toward multifidelity data fusion, task-oriented benchmarks, uncertainty quantification, interpretability and integrated simulation toolchains.

title: From Atoms to Reactors: A Critical Review of a Decade of Machine Learning in Heterogeneous Catalysis (2017–2026)
abstract: ABSTRACT This critical review traces the evolution of machine learning (ML) across the full value chain of heterogeneous catalysis over 2017–2026, from catalyst discovery to reactor and process design, and across the principal reaction families (CO 2 reduction, water splitting, nitrogen chemistry, zeolite‐catalyzed transformations). Each stage is evaluated against four criteria — data foundation, method maturity, experimental validation and deployment readiness — through a structured capability scorecard. Digitalization has advanced from the top of the length scale downward: prediction of adsorption energies and atomistic potential‐energy surfaces is now mature, with errors of tens of meV relative to the reference DFT calculations and accelerations of three orders of magnitude over DFT, yet experimentally validated catalyst improvements remain rare. The most significant advance is the closed‐loop autonomous laboratory coupling Bayesian optimization, automated synthesis and high‐throughput testing. Large language models have begun to add a reasoning and orchestration layer, while kinetics, reactor and process design remain the least digitalized stages. We argue that the field's next decade of impact will be decided not by more accurate atomic‐scale prediction but by carrying ML into experimental validation and the reactor‐and‐process scale, where catalysis is hardest to industrialize and where data‐driven methods are weakest.

title: Boltzmann generators for amorphous particle systems
abstract: Sampling configurations in thermodynamic equilibrium is a long-standing challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann generators address this problem by employing generative models to propose independent configurations, which are then reweighted via importance sampling using exact likelihood evaluations. Recent Boltzmann generators based on continuous normalizing flows and flow matching have achieved significant success for particle systems and biomolecules. However, these approaches have not been extended to amorphous materials (glasses), for which equilibrium sampling is notoriously slow. Because of their disordered structure, the invariances and geometrical constraints of amorphous materials differ from those of crystals and biomolecules, preventing the direct use of existing generative models. Here, we develop Boltzmann generators tailored to amorphous materials by building the required equivariances directly into Riemannian stochastic interpolants. Our framework incorporates periodic boundary conditions and particle symmetries using equivariant graph neural networks. Numerical experiments demonstrate that enforcing physical symmetries significantly improves the accuracy of Boltzmann generators but also reveal an intrinsic limitation of the continuous-flow formulation: accumulated numerical errors during likelihood integration break time-reversibility, compromising exact thermodynamic reweighting. These results reveal a fundamental challenge for continuous-flow generative models in statistical mechanics and call for alternative approaches that preserve exact thermodynamic consistency.

title: Factorised Cartesian Atomic Cluster Expansion for Low-Cost Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials can reach the accuracy of density functional theory at a fraction of its cost, but the most accurate equivariant models remain expensive, mainly because of the tensor operations they perform for every pair of neighbouring atoms. We present FACE, a factorised Cartesian atomic cluster expansion that removes this bottleneck. Each neighbour contributes only a small set of radial functions and messages, and all mixing of feature channels is done once per atom, so the cost per neighbour no longer grows with the size of the model. Custom GPU kernels evaluate the remaining steps, and long-range electrostatics, dispersion and short-range repulsion attach through a single interface. We show that the training divergences we encountered originate in how the network weights are scaled, and we introduce a distillation scheme in which an ensemble generates additional, uncertainty-checked training data. On five rMD17 molecules, with identical training budgets and hardware, FACE is about as accurate as a 64-channel MACE model (over three seeds: better on one molecule, within the seed spread on two, 7–14% higher force errors on two), while it is 5.7 times faster at inference (4.9 times at the same cutoff) and needs 3.5–3.9 times less GPU memory. Training costs about the same per step. Distillation lowers the energy and force errors of a single aspirin model by 20% at fixed width, to 2.26 meV and 6.74 meV/Å, close to the published MACE values (2.2 and 6.6), and the distilled model runs stably in molecular dynamics.

title: Beyond Permeability Prediction: Machine Learning for Gas-Separation Membranes from Data Curation to Experimentally Validated Discovery
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is transforming gas-separation membrane research, yet high retrospective accuracy does not necessarily translate into experimentally viable or process-relevant materials. This review reframes the field around the evidence chain required to convert a membrane record into a defensible discovery decision. Across polymers, metal-organic and covalent organic frameworks, mixed-matrix membranes, carbon molecular sieves, and two-dimensional systems, we critically examine data curation, physics-aligned representation, multitask and multi-fidelity learning, uncertainty quantification, inverse design, and prospective validation. We introduce a five-level evidence framework spanning retrospective interpolation, domain-disjoint generalization, physics or simulation confirmation, prospective membrane validation, and deployment-relevant testing. We further propose a contextualized observation unit that binds chemical identity to membrane state, fabrication history, feed composition, operating conditions, time, protocol, and provenance, thereby exposing leakage and structural uncertainty hidden by conventional datasets. Our analysis shows that ML has demonstrably accelerated data completion, simulation, and candidate prioritization, whereas evidence for routinely discovering manufacturable, durable, mixed-gas-performing membranes remains limited and concentrated in polymer studies. To close this gap, we develop a constrained, uncertainty-aware closed-loop architecture that treats feasibility and fabrication failures as learnable outcomes, couples acquisition to multiscale process utility, and advances candidates through staged experimental fidelities. A minimum reporting standard and measurable research priorities are provided. Together, these contributions propose "decision-grade ML" as an emerging framework for evaluating machine learning in membrane science: models should know their applicability domain, preserve physical context, propose feasible experiments, quantify uncertainty under domain shift, and demonstrate value under the conditions of intended membrane use rather than merely reproduce familiar labels or idealized proxies.

title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity
abstract: Adapting a pre-trained machine-learning interatomic potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity requires improving defect accuracy without degrading the near-equilibrium elastic and vibrational response. Here we achieve this balance for the aluminium MACE potential QP17 by integrating conditional readout uncertainty, iterative full-parameter updates and protocol-compatible relative-energy anchoring. Sensitivities over 144 linear readout weights guide acquisition, with within-batch covariance updates and evolving neural representations. After four active-learning rounds (32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates), force-uncertainty acquisition reduces mean development force error from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Angstrom, outperforming random sampling (22.70), geometry-diversity selection (22.46) and uniform training across all 104 candidate labels (22.71) under the same update budget. All three force-uncertainty runs satisfy bulk-mechanical retention criteria: historical relative-energy error decreases from 0.375 to 0.207 meV/atom, while harmonic phonon root-mean-square drift remains below 0.05 THz. Matched objective ablations reveal that relative-energy anchoring suppresses harmonic drift. Out-of-sample evaluations across planar faults, twin boundaries and grain boundaries demonstrate transferable gains in defect energies and deviatoric stresses, even though virial stresses are never fitted. A closed-loop molecular dynamics and density functional theory (MD-DFT) pilot confirms that automated acceptance gating intercepts updates that violate historical elastic-group energy or vibrational tolerances. Together, these components establish a retention-constrained fine-tuning protocol for improving plastic-deformation observables while preserving the tested bulk mechanical response.

title: Transfer learning on universal interatomic potential embeddings improves generalization in structure-property defect models
abstract: Oxygen vacancy formation energies govern the performance of metal oxides across energy conversion, catalysis, and electronics, yet predicting them accurately without density functional theory calculations for novel chemical systems remains challenging. Here, we show that frozen 256-dimensional embeddings extracted from a pretrained MACE universal machine-learning interatomic potential encode information sufficient to predict vacancy formation energies obtained from density functional theory without requiring supercell construction, vacancy creation, or geometry optimization. A lightweight multilayer perceptron trained on these embeddings (MACE-dGNN) achieves an element-wise cross-validation mean absolute error of 0.38 eV, halving the error of a baseline graph neural network trained from scratch (0.72 eV) and offering a modest advantage over direct MACE relaxation calculations (0.51 eV). Because the embedding approach decouples representation from the prediction task and generalizes well with limited data, it will (1) extend naturally to fine-tuning and prediction of properties (e.g., charged defects) that are inaccessible to generic energy-and force-output interatomic potentials and (2) be trainable on necessarily small datasets, potentially enabling the use of more expensive but accurate tools for generating training data (e.g., hybrid functional calculations) for which training or fine-tuning of interatomic potentials will be difficult. We demonstrate practical impact by revisiting a prior screening of thermochemical water-splitting materials, where improved generalization alters ∼45 % of candidate classifications.

title: Data-driven discovery of water-splitting electrocatalysts: From predictive machine learning to autonomous optimization
abstract: Machine learning is reshaping the design of water-splitting electrocatalysts by enabling data-driven exploration of structure-property relationships beyond conventional trial-and-error approaches. By integrating physically meaningful descriptors with predictive algorithms, ML provides a pathway to accelerate catalyst optimization and uncover underlying reaction mechanisms. Descriptor engineering plays a central role, combining morphological and structural features, composition-dependent chemical descriptors, and electronic structure parameters such as d-band center, density of states, work function, and adsorption energies, together with synthesis-dependent variables linking preparation conditions to performance. On this basis, diverse learning strategies including supervised regression models, ensemble methods, unsupervised clustering, Bayesian optimization, active learning, and deep learning architectures have been employed to navigate complex materials spaces efficiently. Emerging physics-informed and symbolic learning approaches further enhance interpretability while maintaining predictive power. Collectively, these advances accelerate rational catalyst discovery for hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions, improving efficiency in sustainable hydrogen production.

title: Controlling MXene termination ensembles for stability and performance
abstract: Abstract The promise of MXene surface chemistry lies in tuning T $$_{x}$$ x , yet the relevant design variable is not the identity of an individual surface terminating group but the ensemble of local surface environments. In M $$_{n+1}$$ n + 1 X $$_{n}$$ n T $$_{x}$$ x MXenes, where M is an early transition metal and X is C or N, T $$_{x}$$ x is treated here as a functional termination ensemble: the collection of local termination environments that exist across MXene surfaces. These environments are defined by chemical composition, binding-site geometry, coverage, spatial distribution, coordination, defects, intercalants, and edge structures. Because these ensembles evolve during synthesis, storage, processing, and operation, they determine whether MXenes remain structurally intact and functionally useful within application-specific performance–stability windows. We argue that predictive design requires computational approaches that move beyond idealized single-termination models by combining density functional theory, molecular dynamics, statistical sampling, surrogate models, and actively learned machine learning interatomic potentials to map termination ensembles under operating conditions. Coupled with synthesis–characterization feedback, this performance–stability framework links application-defined functions and operating windows to ensembles that can be installed, retained, or deliberately transformed while co-optimizing performance and stability.

title: Autonomous Discovery of Multi‐Material Metamaterials With Programmable Multimodal Thermal Responses via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT Inverse design deep learning models have significantly accelerated materials discovery through mapping complex structure‐property relationships. However, they remain constrained by prohibitive data demands and are limited to in‐distribution interpolation designs. Efficient out‐of‐distribution inverse design under sparse data constraints remains a critical bottleneck. Here we present an inverse design framework integrating Transformer encoder with reinforcement learning (RL) agent. By combining adaptable structural parameterization and hybrid iterative optimization, this framework efficiently navigates the complex, high‐dimensional multi‐material design landscape with extremely low data dependency (<10 3 samples). The inverse design framework leverages reward‐driven mechanism to autonomously evolves multi‐material architectures that achieve unseen target thermal deformation behaviors while strictly adhering to manufacturing requirements. Uniquely, the versatility of this framework is demonstrated through the realization of multiple thermal deformation targets, including near‐zero, negative, and highly anisotropic thermal expansion, as well as complex multimodal deformations. Experimental validation of fabricated structures further confirms the efficacy of our framework for accelerated on‐demand design of multi‐material functional architectures.

title: A thermodynamic correction layer for machine learning interatomic potentials
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials enable atomistic simulations with near \textit{ab initio} accuracy over large length and time scales. Foundation models extend this capability across the periodic table but inherit the thermodynamic description of the electronic structure methods used to generate their training data. Small errors in relative phase stability can therefore produce large errors in transformation temperatures. We introduce an additive thermodynamic correction layer that shifts phase free energies towards an assessed reference without retraining or modifying the base potential. A first order thermodynamic construction converts the required phase free energy shifts directly into configuration energy targets, which are fitted using a linear atomic cluster expansion and refined iteratively from measured free energies. We apply the method to melting and solid to solid transformations across elements with different crystal structures using a foundation GRACE model. After the correction, all transformation temperatures lie within the prescribed tolerance of the assessed values, including Ca, Ti, and Zr, where a solid to solid transition and melting are corrected together. Static energy curves, bulk moduli, and liquid structure remain close to those of the base model. Vacancy formation energies, thermal expansion, and liquid density depend on the corrected phase balance and change where the correction is large. The method requires neither retraining, differentiable dynamics, nor access to the parameters of the base potential. It provides a modular route for combining transferable atomistic models with assessed phase thermodynamics.

title: A systematic review of advances in spatiotemporal machine learning for road traffic accident prediction in developing countries
abstract: Low and middle-income countries (LMICs) account for 93% of global road traffic fatalities, yet spatiotemporal machine learning (ML) research remains structurally anchored in high-income contexts. This review synthesises a global evidence base while directing its analysis toward developing-country road safety: high-income-country studies (34.5%) are retained expressly to quantify, by contrast, the representation gap affecting low- and middle-income countries. This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review applies a dual mandatory inclusion criterion, requiring both a qualifying ML/deep learning algorithm and at least one explicit spatial and/or temporal analytical component, across 58 studies from 22 countries (2020–2026), with methodological quality assessed via PROBAST, marking its first application in road safety ML. Deep learning constituted the largest algorithm category (34.5%), with Random Forest the most frequently used individual algorithm (31.0%). The headline finding that 77.6% of studies employ combined spatiotemporal frameworks conceals substantial heterogeneity: only 17.2% of all studies (10/58) achieve true joint spatiotemporal learning, corresponding to 22.2% of studies within the combined-framework subset (10/45). PROBAST identified the Analysis domain as carrying the highest risk of bias 17.2%, primarily driven by unreported class imbalance handling and, critically, the complete absence of calibration reporting across all 58 studies, a universal limitation undermining model interpretability and deployment readiness. The Research Representation Ratio (RRR), applied here for the first time in road safety ML, suggests a pattern consistent with an inverse relationship between fatality burden and research intensity: high-income countries exhibit an RRR of 5.91 relative to their 7% fatality burden, while Sub-Saharan Africa shows an RRR of 0.27 relative to 26%. Bangladesh (RRR $$\approx $$ 1.15–1.72, roughly proportionate representation once WHO’s country-level fatality estimate is used) has no studies employing network-level GIS or temporal hotspot prediction. A five-priority national research agenda is proposed, addressing topology-aware spatial modeling, temporal hotspot prediction, environmental robustness testing, multi-source data integration, and resource-efficient hybrid modeling via transfer learning from proximate LMIC datasets.

title: Machine learning surrogate modelling for enhanced heat transfer in heat exchangers: A state-of-the-art review
abstract: Complex heat transfer and fluid flow in heat exchangers (HXs) with intricate geometry challenge conventional empirical correlations, while high-fidelity simulations remain computationally expensive. Machine learning (ML)-based surrogate models offer a fast alternative for predicting their thermal–hydraulic behaviour. This review assesses recent studies on ML-based surrogate modelling of HXs with enhanced heat transfer, classified by intensification strategy: (i) passive techniques, such as extended surfaces and surface structuring; (ii) active techniques, such as ultrasonic excitation and pulsating flow; (iii) compact and printed-circuit designs, where additive manufacturing or chemical etching permits internal geometries infeasible by conventional fabrication. Algorithms span regression, tree-based ensembles, support vector machines, artificial neural networks (ANNs) and hybrid physics-informed approaches. Most surrogates reported high accuracy, typically 𝑅 2 > 0 . 9 5 , but predicted only scalar quantities such as Nusselt number, friction factor, pressure drop or outlet temperature. ANNs were the most widely adopted family (35 of 49 studies) and were reported best-performing in 15 of 26 studies comparing them with at least one other algorithm, although ensemble and kernel-based methods proved competitive. The highest accuracies occur in both experimental and CFD-trained work, so no gap attributable to data origin is evident, though the comparison is confounded, since accuracy is measured against whichever source generated the training data. Most studies relied on small, narrowly sampled datasets, and evaluation practices remain inconsistent. Model selection is reported far more consistently than validation design: most partition data at record rather than independent-case level, and only one evaluates the same model under both random and grouped splits, which alone reveals how much reported accuracy is interpolation within a physical case. Multi-output and spatio-temporal surrogates remain rare, and physics-informed approaches appear in only one reviewed study; their claimed data-efficiency and extrapolation advantages derive from the general physics-informed literature and must be weighed against implementation barriers in intensified geometries.

title: SIMPLEX: composition-space deep learning for bio-inspired hydrogel adhesion with prospective validation on model-discovered formulations and interpretable composition rules
abstract: Fast and accurate composition-to-property prediction is critical for accelerating the discovery of multicomponent bio-adhesive hydrogels, yet current surrogate models are predominantly evaluated under random data splits that do not reflect the distribution shift encountered in real-world iterative screening. Moreover, existing deep learning approaches for small-sample formulation data offer little systematic guidance on architecture design and often depend on laboriously engineered interaction features. This study introduces Simplex-Inspired Multimodal Predictive Learning Encoder with X-modal Fusion (SIMPLEX), a dual-modality deep encoder purpose-built for composition-driven property estimation. Its gated multimodal fusion component autonomously learns inter-component interactions without hand-crafted quadratic terms. We establish a fully reproducible benchmark covering eight models with unified hyper-parameter tuning and statistical protocols. Evaluated on 316 internal hydrogel formulations under grouped cross-validation, SIMPLEX achieves first-tier predictive performance, competitive with the strongest classical baselines. On 25 prospectively collected formulations acquired from a Bayesian-optimized closed-loop campaign, a setting that introduces a deliberate distribution shift toward high-performance compositions, SIMPLEX delivers the highest coefficient of determination ( R 2 = 0.6712 ) for adhesion-strength prediction, meeting the demand for precise quantitative estimation in iterative candidate screening. Feature dissection reveals that the native compositional representation already captures the dominant composition–property relationships, and component-wise ablation pinpoints gated multimodal fusion as the principal performance driver. This study delivers a capable deep encoder together with a rigorous, transparent evaluation paradigm for formulation-driven machine learning, providing immediately reusable baselines and design principles for the community.

title: Tangent-plane evidential uncertainty in active learning for magnetic interatomic potentials
abstract: Magnetic interatomic potentials need to account for coupled lattice and spin degrees of freedom, yet constructing reliable training sets remains costly because noncollinear first-principles labels are expensive. Active learning can mitigate this cost, provided that the uncertainty estimate is physically meaningful for the magnetic-response targets that drive spin reorientation. Here we extend the $\mathrm{e}^2\mathrm{IP}$ evidential framework to magnetic machine-learning interatomic potentials by formulating the projected spin-force likelihood and the corresponding epistemic uncertainty in the tangent plane orthogonal to the local spin direction. This construction prevents the uncertainty model from allocating probability mass to a radial spin component that is absent from the constrained-moment supervision. Using bulk BiFeO$_3$ and monolayer CrTe$_2$ as benchmark systems, we show that the resulting tangent-plane epistemic uncertainty indicator $U_{\mathrm{epi}}^{\mathrm{sf}}$ correlates strongly with prediction error and selects more informative configurations than random sampling, simultaneously improving energy, force, and projected spin-force accuracy. These results demonstrate a physically interpretable and data-efficient route for constructing uncertainty-aware magnetic machine-learning interatomic potentials.

title: Interpretable Hybrid Surrogate Modeling for Diameter Deviation Prediction in Injection Molding Using Symbolic Regression and Gaussian Process Residual Correction
abstract: Abstract Dimensional quality in injection molding is hard to model when process variables act through coupled pressure, flow, and cycle-history effects and the experimental budget is small. This study develops an interpretable hybrid surrogate for that setting. The method combines process-informed feature engineering, symbolic regression with PySR, Gaussian Process (GP) residual correction, and surrogate-based optimization. Two design-of-experiments campaigns produced 127 runs, which were consolidated into 27 representative operating conditions by averaging repeated or overlapping conditions. Four controllable variables were retained (holding pressure, counter-pressure, cycle time, and injection speed) and expanded into twelve model inputs through pressure ratios, normalized pressure contrasts, multiplicative interaction terms, and rate-like combinations. A compact symbolic equation selected from the search served as the deterministic baseline. It reached R² = 0.8665 and RMSE = 9.37 µm on the full dataset, and R² = 0.8423 and RMSE = 10.19 µm under leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV). A GP with an RBF + White kernel, trained on the symbolic residuals, lowered the LOOCV RMSE to 9.32 µm and raised R² to 0.8681. Embedding the two surrogates in a Differential Evolution optimizer over the experimentally explored ranges gave predicted minima of about 33.25 µm for the symbolic model and 23.73 µm for the hybrid. These are model-based predictions and were not verified experimentally. The contribution is methodological: a transparent way to pair equation discovery with probabilistic residual refinement when only a few representative operating conditions are available. The framework keeps an explicit analytical core and adds a flexible correction layer and predictive uncertainty for engineering decision support.

title: A provenance-aware zirconia conductivity database and Arrhenius-constrained screening of doped electrolyte candidates
abstract: Abstract Zirconia solid electrolytes are key oxygen-ion conductors, but reported conductivity values depend strongly on dopant chemistry, processing history and measurement temperature. Here we curate a provenance-aware zirconia conductivity database of 1,351 records and use it to compare an Arrhenius-constrained physics-informed machine-learning model (PIML) with an unconstrained deep neural network (DNN). In a reserved grouped-material confirmation split, the DNN achieves the lower pooled root-mean-square error (RMSE, in log 10 σ units) for withheld composition-processing groups. The Arrhenius-constrained model remains on a comparable error scale and provides bounded effective activation-energy estimates. Its clearest benefit appears in matched-material temperature extrapolation: when trained at ≤ 800 • C and tested at ≥ 900 • C (n = 47), PIML reduces RMSE from 0.4187 to 0.3609 and raises R 2 from 0.8562 to 0.8932. Bootstrap analysis supports this record-level gain, with material-fingerprint resampling reported as a conservative uncertainty check. Genetic-algorithm (GA) screening under fixed processing and measurement conditions identifies a Sc-rich/Mg-containing zirconia region. Exploratory CHGNet molecular dynamics provides the main computational ranking check, with single-configuration oxide-reference density functional theory (DFT) retained as an auxiliary thermodynamic screen. This work provides a curated conductivity resource and a conservative screening route for doped zirconia electrolytes.

title: Closed-Loop Reinforcement Learning in De Novo Molecular Design: Bridging Generative AI with Automated Chemical Synthesis
journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
abstract: Closed-loop reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to integrating generative molecular design with automated chemical synthesis and experimental evaluation. However, translating autonomous chemical optimization into pharmaceutical discovery remains challenging because biological measurements are often delayed, variable, and affected by assay limitations. This critical review and perspective examines current autonomous discovery platforms and evaluates the challenges associated with incorporating physical experimental feedback into molecular optimization. It proposes an uncertainty-aware, multi-objective reward architecture and a four-gate qualification framework covering operational synthesizability, analytical identity and purity, biological assay validity, and governed policy updating. Particular attention is given to distinguishing statistically censored measurements from pharmacologically confounded or invalid observations. The article also introduces supervised autonomy as a practical governance approach in which automated systems perform routine experimental operations while scientific experts retain responsibility for critical decisions. The proposed framework provides a foundation for improving the reliability, interpretability, and practical implementation of experimentally informed molecular discovery. Prospective validation remains necessary to establish its effectiveness.

title: Synthesis-by-design of ferroelectric Dion–Jacobson two-dimensional hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites
abstract: Abstract Dion–Jacobson two-dimensional hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites are promising ferroelectric materials, combining chemically tunable polarity enabled by their organic spacers with enhanced environmental stability. However, rational discovery remains difficult owing to uncertain phase formability and scarce, biased ferroelectric data. Here we show a staged, physically guided synthesis-by-design workflow that integrates learning from scarce ferroelectric data with structure-aware screening. Starting from 11 known ferroelectric compounds in this family, symbolic regression defines a descriptor-bounded ferroelectric-consistent region. Similarity-guided expansion and chemical filtering reduce 83,924 molecules to 1012 candidate divalent spacers, while machine-learned interatomic-potential relaxation and connectivity analysis identify 338 candidates retaining Dion–Jacobson connectivity. Sequential prioritization by connectivity retention, chemical similarity, energetic refinement and synthetic accessibility selects s −2-fluorobutane-1,4-diamine, leading to the synthesis of a PbI 4 -based Dion–Jacobson perovskite with experimentally confirmed ferroelectric switching. This prospective proof of concept shows how sparse property knowledge can be coupled with structural screening to prioritize organic spacer candidates for experimental synthesis.

title: Multi-Fidelity Training Reshapes Uncertainty Decomposition in Atomistic Models
abstract: Multi-fidelity training, which combines abundant low-fidelity data with scarce high-fidelity labels, is increasingly common in atomistic modeling, but its effect on predictive uncertainty remains largely unexplored. We investigate this question using deep ensembles of mean-variance MACE models trained on ANI-1x, contrasting high-fidelity training from scratch with low-fidelity pretraining followed by fine-tuning. We characterize aleatoric, epistemic, and total uncertainty throughout training and under two distribution shifts: unseen molecular systems and higher-energy configurations. We find that pretraining reduces prediction error and improves uncertainty-based ranking across all test sets, but does not yield well-calibrated predictive variances; calibration deteriorates more severely under energy extrapolation. Training-dynamics analysis localizes most of this calibration degradation to high-fidelity optimization, during which the learned aleatoric variance becomes overconfident on held-out data. Moreover, multi-fidelity fine-tuning produces a more effective uncertainty-based acquisition function than high-fidelity training from scratch. These findings show that uncertainty ranking and calibration capture distinct properties and must be assessed separately in multi-fidelity atomistic models, especially under extrapolation.

title: Physicochemical rule-embedded generative modeling for constrained peptide therapeutics
abstract: Constrained peptides couple covalent topology, stereochemistry, three-dimensional structure, conformational dynamics and developability. We review physicochemical rule embedding across chemical-language, target-conditioned structural, geometric, atom-bond, ensemble and property-guided generative models, distinguishing generated molecular objects from downstream inference and predictions from prospective evidence. We identify limitations in chemical coverage, applicability, uncertainty and pipeline attribution, and routes towards identity-preserving, environment-aware and experimentally calibrated design.

title: Infrastructure-Aware Materials Discovery: Resource Allocation, Cost, and Carbon in AI-Driven Workflows
abstract: Abstract Machine-learned interatomic potentials have converted materials-discovery campaigns from tens to hundreds of expensive density-functional calculations into populations of 10^4 to 10^6 short, independent evaluations, relocating the dominant constraint from the electronic-structure solver to the orchestration layer beneath it. We organize AI-driven materials-discovery workloads into four recurring classes—short independent screening tasks, long-running simulations, tightly coupled ab initio calculations, and iterative active-learning loops—and map spot and preemptible computing, checkpointing and workflow-level fault tolerance, autoscaling, cloud bursting, cost-aware Bayesian optimization, and carbon-aware scheduling against this taxonomy. High-throughput screening of metal–organic frameworks serves as a case study arguing that the optimal balance of elastic, stable, and interruptible resources follows from task duration, computational coupling, and recovery cost rather than from generic cloud-optimization heuristics. We further argue that the realized cost of a materials calculation decomposes into scientific, provisioning, recovery, and data-movement terms, of which only the first is a property of the calculation itself. Because the remaining terms vary with market and grid conditions on timescales of minutes, an acquisition function that prices candidates by fidelity alone systematically misprices the campaign it is scheduling. Integrating infrastructure cost and carbon signals into scientific decision-making is identified as a key open problem for autonomous discovery.

title: Active Learning of Conditional Generative Models via the Transport Neural Tangent Kernel
abstract: Many high-throughput scientific experiments produce distributional outputs, requiring conditional generative models to interpret the data, and to predict outcomes at new inputs. Acquiring experimental data at new conditions (e.g., for a new antigen or a new cell type) is often expensive, motivating the need for automated experimental design methods. However, existing active learning frameworks are limited as they assume scalar or vector-valued outputs. We first show that the Wasserstein test risk of a conditional generative task decomposes into a mean term and a shape term, demonstrating why mean-based active learning is blind to distributional shape. To capture both, we propose the transport Neural Tangent Kernel (tNTK), a tractable kernel that measures how sensitive a generative model's predicted distribution is with respect to its parameters. The tNTK recovers the standard NTK in the deterministic limit and upper-bounds the posterior Fréchet variance of the prediction under small parameter perturbations. It admits a closed-form expression for affine Gaussian transport and tractable Monte Carlo estimators otherwise. Treating the tNTK as the covariance function of a Gaussian process, we greedily select inputs that minimize the total GP posterior variance across the pool, yielding a distribution-aware active learning strategy. We evaluate this strategy across four classes of conditional generative models, including conditional flow matching and conditional Monge gap, on synthetic distributions, intent-labeled sentences, and single-cell perturbation responses. In these experiments, the tNTK outperforms the baseline NTK computed from the conditional mean, demonstrating the value of distribution-aware active learning for generative-modeling tasks.

title: Building from the ground up: augmentation strategies to improve protein language model performance on protein sets
abstract: Abstract An important underlying requirement for deep learning models is the availability of large datasets, however, in sciences such as chemistry and biology, generating experimental data of sufficient size represents a significant bottleneck. In this work, we probed the extent and nature of limited input data, characterize how several protein language models (pLMs) learned on suboptimal datasets, and investigated augmentation approaches to improve predictive model performance. We found that narrowing the distribution of protein-protein complexes in a limited dataset permits an order-ofmagnitude decrease in training dataset size, if a model is only expected to generalize to in-distribution data. Similar results were found in active learning (AL), where both inand out-of-distribution Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) showed a small but consistent increase upon augmentation of the training set with complexes produced by ESM-3, a generative pLM.

title: Probing the limits of forward screening and inverse design of crystal materials
abstract: Crystal materials are designed either by screening known crystals for a target property or by generating new crystals with that property. Both routes are judged against public databases of known crystals, but these databases name the same crystal differently. Several materials announced as new by recent generative and autonomous discovery campaigns have since proved to be known phases or close variants of them. The limits of both routes remain unmeasured. Here we probe them by matching the crystals of 55 databases by structure into one self-extending database of 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values, each traced to its source. Only 4.5% of its crystal-property pairs carry a value. To fill the empty pairs, we developed CGTNet, an equivariant graph transformer with state-of-the-art accuracy on several tasks of two public benchmarks. Trained on each task, it forms a library of property models whose predictions we release. The reach of forward screening has been underestimated. Known crystals hold tens of thousands of ultra-incompressible candidates without a recorded bulk modulus, and a post hoc audit of synthesis evidence finds among them ReN2, whose bulk modulus was measured at 428 GPa. The novelty claimed for inverse design has been overestimated. At an equal verification budget, a stiffness-conditioned generator returned more stiff hits than screening (100 versus 55), but all contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions. Integrating and completing the databases of known crystals therefore moves the limits of both routes: it widens what screening can reach and sets the reference against which generated crystals are judged new.

title: Hierarchical universal open structure dataset for atomistic modeling
abstract: Atomic-scale simulations have been transformed by machine-learning models that predict the properties of atomistic structures with the accuracy of quantum calculations, but at a small fraction of the cost. These models have increased dramatically in generality, thanks to the availability of synthetic datasets of ever-increasing size and scope. The proliferation of datasets, with properties often computed using different levels of electronic-structure approximation, is problematic, as there is often overlap between different datasets, and strong correlations between structures obtained with short molecular dynamics trajectories or geometry optimization. To address these problems, we introduce a protocol to stratify a dataset into a hierarchy of nested subsets, subsampling from the coarsest to the finest resolution based on an "ecumetric" built to reflect the latent space representation of several popular universal machine-learning interatomic potentials. We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose $2^{24}$ most diverse members form the MAD-CORE stratified coreset, which can be easily used for all sorts of tasks, from exploratory experiments to the training of foundation models at scale. We envision that this collection will guide and help coordinate future efforts, focusing them on the most relevant and/or undersampled regions of chemical and structural space, and that it will be further extended to incorporate the outcomes of the collective work of this community.

title: Orochi: A Physics-Grounded Python Package for Pair Distribution Function Analysis of Crystalline and Low-Dimensional Materials
abstract: Atomic pair distribution function (PDF) analysis from X-ray total scattering is a powerful methodology for determining atomic structure and arrangements across crystalline, disordered, nanostructured, and low-dimensional materials on both laboratory and synchrotron instruments. Fundamentally, PDF analysis relies on two core pillars—PDF data reduction from one-dimensional (1D) total scattering profiles and real-space structural modeling—often accompanied in rapid-acquisition experiments by upstream two-dimensional (2D) detector image processing. However, conventional workflows remain fragmented across disconnected software tools, forcing researchers to manually combine multiple programs and preventing the simultaneous optimization of measurement reduction parameters and crystal structure parameters that is standard in X-ray Rietveld refinement. Furthermore, mainstream PDF modeling engines rely on legacy physical approximations: they enforce three-dimensional (3D) periodic boundary conditions (requiring artificial vacuum supercells for 2D nanosheets), treat atomic scattering factors as angle-independent constants (causing peak distortions in compounds with large atomic number contrast), and approximate number density baselines using macroscopic bulk volume assumptions. Here, the open-source, pure-Python architecture of Orochi (version 4.0) is presented, implementing physical calculations from scratch in Python (accelerated via Numba) to unify total scattering data reduction, symmetry-aware crystallographic modeling, and real-space PDF simulation alongside a dedicated high-Q 2D detector processing module within a self-contained Python environment. Originally developed for laboratory total scattering studies of pharmaceutical glasses and deployed as compiled executable (β-version) tools at SPring-8 beamlines, Orochi has been completely redesigned around an externalized parameter management core (orochi.base) in which parameters are stored in standardized Python dictionaries and accessed via hierarchical string addresses. By bringing parameters outside the calculation engines rather than locking them inside built-in optimizers, this architecture allows multiple module instances across data reduction and structural modeling to be optimized simultaneously by modern optimization algorithms, machine learning libraries, and autonomous AI agents. For structural simulation, intra-cell atomic pair vectors are decoupled from lattice translation vectors to natively support arbitrary periodic boundary conditions across 3D crystals, 2D nanosheets, 1D nanowires, and 0D clusters. The simulation engine incorporates the full scattering vector (Q) dependence of atomic form factors, enabling accurate modeling of heavy/light-element oxides and permitting direct instrumental calibration using standard CeO2 powder rather than monoatomic nickel substitutes. Furthermore, a sinc-convolution density formulation is established to accurately reproduce baseline ripples arising from finite Qmin cutoffs in nanostructured systems. Complete mathematical formulations for all reduction and simulation algorithms are consolidated to establish a rigorous foundation for automated crystallographic analysis.

title: Artificial intelligence in offshore wind geotechnical engineering: A lifecycle-oriented review
abstract: Abstract As offshore wind develops toward deeper waters and larger turbine capacities, geotechnical challenges are becoming increasingly complex, involving more variable seabed conditions, larger foundation dimensions, and stricter lifecycle reliability and cost-control requirements. Accordingly, artificial intelligence (AI), with strengths in data fusion, surrogate modeling, and monitoring-informed inference, has increasingly been explored as a complementary computational and analytical tool in offshore wind geotechnical engineering. Particular attention is given to spatially variable ground characterization, surrogate-based response and reliability assessment, and monitoring-informed evaluation of installation and service states. This paper presents a lifecycle-oriented review of AI applications, informed by systematically screened research articles published between 2001 and 2025 and selected project- and industry-level practices. The main AI application pathways are synthesized across site investigation, foundation design, installation, and operation and maintenance (O&M), and are related to stage-specific geotechnical problems rather than algorithm categories alone. The synthesis shows a differentiated maturity pattern across the lifecycle. Foundation design shows the highest research concentration, while project-level digital ground modeling in site investigation and design-stage surrogate analysis show the clearest pathways to engineering use. Closed-loop installation control and below-mudline state inference for O&M remain largely at the research or validation stage. Across these applications, several cross-cutting limitations remain, including sparse offshore data, insufficient physical constraints, limited cross-site generalizability, incomplete standardization, and limited engineering acceptance. Future directions are discussed, including physics-integrated models, high-quality data ecosystems supported by standardized benchmark datasets, certification-oriented validation, and reviewable agent-assisted workflows to support more reliable and cost-effective offshore wind development.
